references.text: The people of Israel ate sacrifices to idols and bowed down to them, showing the same idolatry mentioned in Deuteronomy 32:38
Joshua urges the people to remove foreign gods, which are the same gods that ate their sacrificial fat and drank their drink offerings
Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal and suggests that their god may be sleeping, similar to the ironic challenge for idols to rise up and help
Isaiah describes Israel's idolatry with drink offerings and food sacrifices to other gods, the same theme found in Deuteronomy 32:38
Jeremiah mentions that the people bake cakes for the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to foreign gods
The people admit they brought drink offerings and incense to the queen of heaven, a direct parallel to the idol sacrifices in Deuteronomy
The psalmist describes the powerlessness of idols—they cannot see, hear, or help—the same irony as in the challenge for gods to rise up and be a refuge
Paul warns against having fellowship with demons through pagan sacrifices and drink offerings, a New Testament parallel to warnings against idol sacrifices
